You are a blind semantic decoder of a natural-language crystal description. The user message is your only source of material-specific information. Understand the spatial narrative and produce a construction plan; do not guess missing independent numbers or look up a material. Return one JSON object only, without Markdown fences.
For sufficient information use:
{"status":"ok","space_group_number":integer,"hall_symbol":"Hall symbol stated in the text","lattice":[input_a,input_b,input_c,input_alpha,input_beta,input_gamma],"composition":{"Element":input_cell_atom_count},"orbits":[{"element":"Element","wyckoff":"multiplicity_and_letter","representative":[standard_fractional_x,standard_fractional_y,standard_fractional_z]}],"frame_transform":{"matrix":[[p11,p12,p13],[p21,p22,p23],[p31,p32,p33]],"origin_shift":[s1,s2,s3]},"round_digits":integer_or_null,"precision_corrections":[{"element":"Element","at":[input_fractional_x_before_correction,input_fractional_y_before_correction,input_fractional_z_before_correction],"delta":[fractional_dx,fractional_dy,fractional_dz]}]}
Lengths use angstroms, angles use degrees. The specified lattice and composition refer to the original input cell. Orbit representatives refer to the standard Hall coordinate frame. Copy the Hall symbol as a mathematical identifier rather than guessing a public-table integer number. Any equivalent representative of a declared orbit is allowed. Distinct independent orbits of the same element remain separate.
The geometry engine expands the public Hall symmetry orbits, applies q_input = inverse(P)(q_standard - s), selects images in the input cell, rounds fractional coordinates if round_digits is given, and applies precision corrections at their identified input-frame atom positions. If the text explicitly uses identical frames, supply identity P and zero shift. If no rounding is specified, use null. If no corrections are specified, use an empty array. All sites have full occupancy.
Numerical relations in the prose should be resolved into numbers in the plan. Do not silently replace the original geometry with an idealized one. For missing required information return {"status":"insufficient_information","reason":"..."}; for contradictory constraints return {"status":"conflict","reason":"..."}. Your input contains no source CIF or hidden data. Public crystallographic definitions are allowed; material-specific external retrieval is not.

The structure is described in the tetragonal space group I4mm, space-group number 107, with Hall symbol I 4 -2. The input cell is not the conventional tetragonal cell: it is a rhombohedral-like setting with all three input lattice lengths equal to 15.22430527 Å, two interaxial angles equal to 164.89460832°, and the third angle equal to 21.42504624°. The declared input composition is Sr1Bi3Br3O4, corresponding to 11 atoms in the supplied input cell. Fractional coordinates are used, and the standard and input frames are related by q_standard = P q_input + s. The transformation matrix P has rows (0.5, −0.5, 0.5), (0.5, −0.5, −0.5), and (0.5, 0.5, −0.5), while the origin shift s is zero to numerical precision, with components on the order of ±5.6 × 10−17. No positional corrections were applied beyond this frame description, and the positional values are rounded to six decimal places.

In the standard I4mm description, the structure is built from seven independent two-fold sites on the polar fourfold axis and two independent four-fold oxygen sites. All seven two-fold orbits lie on Wyckoff position 2a with coordinate relation (0, 0, z), so each contributes one atom at the representative height and a symmetry-equivalent partner generated by the body-centered tetragonal symmetry. Strontium occupies one such axial orbit at z = 0.658441. Bismuth is distributed over three inequivalent axial orbits rather than a single site: the three independent Bi heights are z = 0.929115, z = 0.075755, and z = 0.345588. Bromine likewise occupies three independent axial orbits, at z = 0.797941, z = 0.212318, and z = 0.486310. Thus the c-axis contains a sequence of distinct Sr, Bi, and Br layers, with each 2a orbit repeated according to the I4mm symmetry.

Oxygen occupies two independent 4b orbits with coordinate relation (0, 1/2, z). The first oxygen orbit has representative position (0, 1/2, 0.389035), and the second has representative position (0, 1/2, 0.108231). Because these are four-fold sites, each oxygen parameter set generates four symmetry-related atoms in the conventional cell, giving eight oxygen atoms in the standard-cell description. Together with the seven two-fold axial orbits, these positions define the full independent atomic geometry: one Sr orbit, three inequivalent Bi orbits, three inequivalent Br orbits, and two inequivalent O orbits, all expressed in the I4mm standard frame and recoverable in the original input cell through the stated transformation.
